stem: What was the most important long-term effect of granting railroads alternate sections of land along their lines?

stimulus.source_note: Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862, 12 Stat. 489, Sec. 3. Public domain. Text verified against the Gilder Lehrman excerpt (Our Documents) and the Supreme Court's quotation of Sec. 3 in Platt v. Union Pacific Railroad Co., 99 U.S. 48 (1878).
stimulus.text:
Pacific Railway Act of 1862, Section 3 (ellipses mark omissions):

"That there be, and is hereby, granted to the said company, for the purpose of aiding in the construction of said railroad and telegraph line, and to secure the safe and speedy transportation of the mails, troops, munitions of war, and public stores thereon, every alternate section of public land, designated by odd numbers, to the amount of five alternate sections per mile on each side of said railroad, on the line thereof, and within the limits of ten miles on each side of said road, not sold, reserved, or otherwise disposed of by the United States, and to which a preemption or homestead claim may not have attached, at the time the line of said road is definitely fixed: Provided, That all mineral lands shall be excepted from the operation of this act..."

options.text: The railroads became great landowners who shaped where towns grew and who could settle nearby
The railroads were forced to give their land back to the government after three years
options.misconception: Background: unsold grant land became open to settlement at $1.25 an acre, but the companies kept what they sold; nothing was simply handed back.

options.text: The railroads stopped carrying freight and carried only passengers
options.misconception: Background: freight was the railroads' main business; carrying wheat, cattle, and goods east paid for the lines.

options.text: The government collected all the profits from selling railroad land
options.misconception: Background: the companies sold their grant land and kept the money; Barron's puts the take at about $435 million.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the grants totaled more than 175 million acres, and the companies sold much of it, promoted settlement along their lines, and watched towns rise where the tracks ran. Land made the railroads settlers' landlords as well as their carriers.
rationales.B: Background: Section 3 said unsold lands would open to settlement at up to $1.25 an acre after three years, but land the companies had already sold stayed sold.
rationales.C: Background: freight paid the bills. Wheat, cattle, and manufactured goods rode the rails east and west; passengers were the smaller business.
rationales.D: Background: the companies kept the proceeds of their land sales, about $435 million by Barron's count. The government took no share of the sales.
rationales.general:
A grant of land is never just a gift; it is a map of who will own the future.
1. Count the scale in Section 3: five alternate sections per mile, on both sides, for hundreds of miles.
2. Follow what the companies did with it. Background: they sold the land, advertised it in eastern cities, and towns grew up along the tracks.
3. Name the lasting effect. The railroads decided who settled where, because they owned the ground beside the road.
Remember: whoever owns the land beside the road decides where the towns go.
